questions.prompt: A reporting transaction runs `SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'new'` twice. The first run returns 12, the second returns 14, because another transaction committed two matching inserts in between. Which anomaly is this?
options: A dirty read
A non-repeatable read
A phantom read
A lost update
questions.explanation:
The distinction that matters is what changed. A phantom read occurs when the *set of rows matching a predicate* changes between two reads in the same transaction. A non-repeatable read occurs when a *value inside a row you already read* changes. Here no row the transaction saw was modified; new rows appeared that satisfy `status = 'new'`. That is a phantom.

"A non-repeatable read" is the most-chosen wrong answer, and the misconception behind it is real: people treat any changed query result as the same anomaly, collapsing row-level and predicate-level effects into one idea. The reason the distinction exists is that they need different defences — row versioning is enough to stop a non-repeatable read, but stopping a phantom requires reasoning about rows that do not exist yet. "A dirty read" encodes the belief that seeing any concurrency effect mid-transaction means you saw uncommitted data; the inserts here were committed, which is precisely why they became visible. "A lost update" is the reflex of treating every anomaly name as interchangeable: a lost update requires two transactions writing the same row, and this transaction writes nothing at all.

What the defence costs: preventing phantoms means the engine must lock or track ranges that hold no rows, or give the transaction a frozen snapshot for its whole lifetime. Range locking suppresses concurrent inserts into the range, which is a direct throughput cost; a long-lived snapshot holds back reclamation of old row versions, which is a storage and maintenance cost. This is why engines default to a level that permits phantoms and make you opt in.

One assumption worth naming: this anomaly is possible at the default isolation level of many engines, but not all defaults behave the same way. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read forbids phantom reads entirely — stronger than the SQL standard requires at that level — because the standard specifies which anomalies must *not* occur, and exceeding it is conformant.

questions.prompt: In a log-structured merge engine, one key's data is written to disk several times over its lifetime as background compaction merges sorted files into larger ones. Which cost does this repeated rewriting measure?
options: Write amplification
Read amplification
Space amplification
Write stalling
questions.explanation:
Write amplification is the ratio of bytes the storage device actually writes to bytes the application asked to write. Compaction is the source of it in an LSM engine: a record written once by the application is rewritten each time it is merged into a higher level, so a key can be written to disk five or ten times before it settles.

"Read amplification" is the sibling metric and the most common confusion — it counts how many disk reads one logical read costs, which in an LSM engine is high for a different reason: a lookup may have to check the in-memory table plus several levels of sorted files. "Space amplification" is the third member of the same family and the closest near-miss here, because compaction does affect it; but space amplification measures bytes on disk against live logical bytes, which grows from obsolete versions *waiting* for compaction rather than from the rewriting itself. "Write stalling" names the symptom rather than the cost: when compaction cannot keep pace with ingest, the engine throttles or blocks incoming writes. You can have high write amplification with no stalls at all, so the two are not the same measurement.

These three amplifications trade against each other, and no engine minimises all of them at once — that is the useful principle to carry away. An LSM engine buys a cheap, sequential write path and good compression of sorted blocks, and pays in read amplification and compaction I/O that competes with foreground traffic. A B-tree pays its own amplification differently: updating one row dirties and eventually writes a whole page, so a small random update can cost a multiple of its size, but there is no compaction backlog and no stall behaviour to tune.

The practical consequence: if your workload is read-dominated and fits in memory, LSM's write-path advantage buys you almost nothing while its compaction still competes for I/O and disturbs your latency tail.

questions.prompt: A query selects only the columns `user_id` and `status`. An index on `(user_id, status)` lets the database answer it entirely from the index, without reading the table's row storage. What is this access called?
options: A clustered index scan
An index-only scan
A partial index scan
A bitmap index scan
questions.explanation:
The property being tested is *coverage*: whether every column the query needs is present in the index itself. When it is, the engine can answer from the index alone and skip the second lookup into row storage, which is where most of the I/O in an indexed query usually goes. An index with this property is commonly called a covering index, and the access it enables is an index-only scan.

Each wrong option names a real mechanism that people reach for by word association. "A clustered index scan" describes where the *rows themselves* physically live — InnoDB stores table rows in primary-key order, so its primary key is clustered — which is a statement about storage layout, not about which columns an index happens to contain. "A partial index scan" is the trap the word *partial* sets: a partial index covers a subset of **rows**, defined by a predicate, not a subset of columns. Confusing the two is common enough that it is worth naming explicitly. "A bitmap index scan" is a planner strategy for collecting many row locations, combining them across indexes, and sorting them before fetching — which by definition still visits row storage, so it is the opposite of what is described.

What coverage costs: every column you add to an index is another column to maintain on every update of that row, and a wider index stores fewer entries per page, so a scan reads more pages to cover the same number of rows. Adding a column purely to make one query index-only is often a bad trade — you slow every write to that table to speed one read path.

One engine-specific caveat that matters in practice: in PostgreSQL the index carries no visibility information, so an index-only scan checks the visibility map for each candidate row's page. If the page is not marked all-visible the engine must visit the row after all, and the scan gains no advantage over an ordinary index scan. A perfectly covering index on a heavily updated table can therefore deliver none of the benefit until the table is vacuumed.

questions.prompt: A transaction inserts three rows, and the database process is killed before the transaction commits. After restart, none of the three rows exist. Which property does this outcome demonstrate?
options: Consistency
Durability
Isolation
Atomicity
questions.explanation:
Atomicity is the guarantee that a transaction's effects are all-or-nothing: partial work never becomes visible, including across a crash. Three rows were written and none survived, because the transaction never committed, so the recovery process discarded them. That is atomicity doing its job.

"Durability" is the answer most people give, and the misconception is precise enough to be worth naming: durability says that once a commit is *acknowledged*, its effects survive a crash. It says nothing whatsoever about uncommitted work. Because the scenario involves a crash and a correct-looking outcome, it reads as durability — but the transaction here was never acknowledged, so durability was never engaged. "Consistency" is the letter of ACID that carries the least independent meaning and attracts the most misuse; in its technical sense it means a transaction moves the database from one state satisfying its declared constraints to another, which is a statement about constraint enforcement, not crash behaviour. "Isolation" concerns what *concurrent* transactions can observe about each other, and there is no second transaction in this scenario at all.

The mechanism behind both atomicity and durability is the same write-ahead log, which is why they get conflated. Before a change touches the data pages, a record of it goes to the log; on restart, the engine replays committed transactions forward and rolls uncommitted ones back. Durability is the replay direction, atomicity is the rollback direction.

What atomicity costs: the logging and undo bookkeeping is paid by every transaction, whether it commits or not. A long transaction that aborts makes the engine do work it then discards, and in a multi-version engine it also holds back cleanup of old row versions for its whole lifetime — so an abandoned transaction is not free just because it changed nothing.

questions.prompt: A table has one index, on `(tenant_id, created_at)`. Which query can use it both to locate rows and to return them already ordered, with no separate sort step?
options: `WHERE created_at > '2026-01-01' ORDER BY tenant_id`
`WHERE tenant_id > 42 ORDER BY created_at`
`WHERE tenant_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at`
`WHERE tenant_id = 42 ORDER BY total DESC`
questions.explanation:
A composite index is sorted lexicographically by its column list, and that single fact answers the question. `created_at` is ordered only *within* one value of `tenant_id`. Pin `tenant_id` to a single value with an equality predicate and you land on one contiguous run of the index in which `created_at` is already in order, so the engine can walk it and stop early.

The first option, filtering on `created_at` and ordering by `tenant_id`, encodes the belief that a composite index behaves like a bag of independent single-column indexes usable in any role. It does not: without a constraint on the leading column, there is no way to seek, and the index offers no advantage over scanning. The second option is the subtle one and the reason this question exists: a *range* on the leading column spans many `tenant_id` values, and while `created_at` is ordered inside each of them, it is not ordered across them, so a global ordering still requires a sort. The misconception is that any predicate on the leading column preserves the second column's ordering, when only equality does. The fourth option encodes the belief that once an index satisfies the filter, the sort comes free regardless of which column is sorted — `total` is not in the index, so the ordering must be computed.

One honest qualification, because it is the difference between a rule and a superstition: this describes a single index scan. Some planners can recover ordering for a range or an `IN` list by scanning each matching value separately and merging the results — PostgreSQL can produce a merge over per-value scans in some plans. So "a range on the leading column forces a sort" is the general case and the right default assumption, not an absolute law.

What this index costs: it serves "newest rows for one tenant" extremely well and cannot serve "newest rows across all tenants" at all. If you need both, you need a second index or a different physical layout, and you pay for that on every write.

questions.prompt: Users post a comment and are redirected to a page served from an asynchronous read replica. Replication lag is normally 50 ms but reaches 4 s under load, and users report that their own comment is missing. Which change most directly guarantees a user sees their own writes?
options: Add more read replicas so load per replica falls and lag shrinks
Make the replica synchronous, so commits wait for it to apply the write
Retry the read after a short delay until the comment becomes visible
Route a user's reads to the primary briefly after that user writes
questions.explanation:
Read-your-writes is a *session* guarantee, not a global one, and that is the whole insight. It only has to hold for the one user who just wrote, so it can be bought per session rather than by strengthening the entire system. Sending that user's reads to the primary — or to a replica proven to have applied past the write's log position — restores the guarantee at the cost of a little primary read load, and only for users who wrote recently.

"Add more read replicas" mistakes lag for a throughput problem. Replicas reduce per-replica *query* load, but lag is driven by the primary's write rate against the replica's apply rate, and apply is often far less parallel than the writes that produced it. Adding replicas frequently does not reduce lag at all, and never bounds it. "Retry the read after a short delay" treats an unbounded staleness window as something a client loop can paper over; it converts a correctness problem into an unbounded latency problem, and in the 4-second tail the user simply waits 4 seconds.

Making the replica synchronous is the genuinely defensible runner-up, and it deserves credit rather than dismissal: it does fix the symptom, for every session, with no routing logic. What it costs is that *every* writer everywhere now pays replication latency on commit, and the primary's ability to accept writes becomes coupled to the standby's health — a slow disk on the standby becomes a slow write path for the whole application. If your durability requirements already demand synchronous replication, take it and get read-your-writes for free; if they do not, you have made every write slower to fix a read problem affecting one user at a time.

What the correct answer costs: primary read capacity, plus a policy for how long the window lasts. Too short and you still miss writes; too long and most traffic lands on the primary, defeating the replicas. The precise version tracks each session's last write position and picks any replica that has passed it, which costs plumbing but bounds the primary load properly.

questions.prompt: A booking system must handle 300 bookings/s at peak, will hold about 40 GB after three years, has substantial ad-hoc reporting requirements, and must never allocate the same resource twice. Which primary datastore fits best?
options: A document database, with each booking as a self-contained document
A single relational database with appropriate indexes
A wide-column store partitioned by resource identifier
A relational database sharded by resource identifier from the start
questions.explanation:
Choose the store from the binding constraint, and here the binding constraint is not volume. 300 writes/s and 40 GB fit comfortably on one well-provisioned relational instance — that is a small database by any modern measure. The hard parts are a correctness invariant that spans rows (no resource allocated twice, under concurrent attempts) and ad-hoc reporting. A single relational database gives you both nearly for free: transactions at an isolation level strong enough to enforce the invariant, and SQL for the reports.

The document option is attractive because a booking really does look like a self-contained document, and if each booking were independent it would be a fine choice. The misconception is that per-document atomicity is enough: the invariant is *across* bookings competing for the same resource, which is exactly what a document-scoped atomicity model does not cover. You end up reimplementing reservation and conflict detection in application code. The wide-column option encodes the belief that partitioning by the contended key is a scalability win — it is, for raw throughput, but it gives you no cross-row transaction, so the contention you partitioned for becomes application-level compare-and-set, and reporting needs a second system entirely.

Sharding the relational database from day one is the most defensible wrong answer, and the misconception is the most respectable: that sharding early is cheap insurance against future growth. It is not cheap. You pay permanently in cross-shard transactions, query complexity and operational surface, to solve a volume problem that does not exist at 40 GB and may never exist.

What the correct answer honestly costs: one instance is one failure domain and one ceiling. You will need replicas for read scale and failover, and you are accepting that some future growth may force a migration. That is usually the better trade — paying distributed-transaction complexity for three years to avoid a migration you may never need is a worse deal than doing the migration if and when the numbers demand it. If the numbers were 300,000 bookings/s or 40 TB, this answer flips.

questions.prompt: You replace a B-tree storage engine with a log-structured merge engine using leveled compaction, keeping the same hardware and the same workload. Which effects should you expect?
options: A point lookup may have to check several files on disk, making bloom filters load-bearing
Random-insert throughput improves, because writes are batched and written sequentially
Disk usage can exceed the live dataset size until compaction catches up
Range scans over a key prefix become impossible without a secondary index
Reads never observe data that compaction has not yet merged
questions.explanation:
The three correct statements are the three consequences of the same design decision: an LSM engine never updates in place, so a key's current value may live in the in-memory table or in any of several on-disk levels, and obsolete versions persist until compaction removes them.

That structure is why a point lookup may check the memtable and then one file per level, which is read amplification, and why bloom filters stop being an optimisation and become structural — without them, every miss pays a disk read at every level. It is also why random-insert throughput improves: the engine buffers writes in memory and flushes sorted runs sequentially, converting the scattered page writes a B-tree would perform into large sequential ones. And it is why on-disk size can exceed the live dataset: superseded versions and tombstones occupy space until a compaction merges them away, which is space amplification.

"Range scans become impossible without a secondary index" encodes a genuinely common misconception — that log-structured means unordered, as if the engine were hash-based. The files are sorted runs; that is what the *merge* in the name refers to. A range scan is a merged iteration across levels, which costs more than a B-tree's leaf traversal but is entirely supported and is one of the reasons LSM engines are used for ordered key-value workloads at all. "Reads never observe unmerged data" inverts the mechanism: a read *must* consult unmerged data, because the newest version of a key is precisely the one that has not yet been compacted downward. If reads only saw compacted data they would serve stale values.

What the swap costs overall: you trade a predictable write path for a cheaper one with a background process that competes with foreground traffic. When compaction falls behind, the engine throttles ingest and your latency tail moves — a failure mode B-trees do not have. The gain is real for write-heavy and ingest-heavy work; for a read-dominated workload that fits in memory, you have taken on tail-latency risk in exchange for very little.

questions.prompt: You must rename a column from `email` to `contact_email` on a table read and written by a fleet of application servers that deploy gradually. There must be no read or write downtime, and it must be possible to stop and reverse at any step. Put the steps in order.
items: Deploy code that writes both columns and reads the old column
Add the new column as nullable, with no application change
Backfill the new column for existing rows, in batches
Deploy code that reads the new column and still writes both
Deploy code that reads and writes only the new column
questions.explanation:
The constraint that fixes this order is that deploys are gradual, so at every moment two versions of the application are running against one schema. Each step must therefore be safe with both its predecessor and its successor live.

Adding a nullable column is invisible to code that does not know about it, so it goes first and is safe on its own. Dual-writing must come before the backfill, and this is the step people invert: if you backfill first, every row written between the backfill and the dual-write deploy has an empty new column, and you would have to backfill again. Once all writers populate both columns, the backfill has no moving target and can run in batches without a consistent-snapshot requirement. Reading the new column comes only after the backfill completes, and writes stay dual so that a rollback to the previous version still finds the old column populated. Only when no deployed version references the old column is it safe to drop, and dropping is the one irreversible step, which is why it is last.

The property this buys is that every step before the last can be reverted by redeploying the previous version, with no data loss. That is the actual point of the sequence — not the renaming, which a single statement could do, but the reversibility.

What it costs: five or six deploys, a period where the table carries duplicated data, and application code carrying a dual-write path. Dual-write paths drift; someone adds a write site that updates only one column, and you get silent divergence that the backfill has already finished covering. For a small table on a system that can tolerate a brief lock, a single `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN` with a coordinated deploy is dramatically cheaper and is the right answer. This sequence earns its complexity only when downtime is genuinely unacceptable and the table is large enough that the rewrite or lock would be long.

One engine-specific note: whether adding a column is cheap depends on the column definition. In current PostgreSQL, adding a column with no default or with a non-volatile default does not rewrite the table — the default is evaluated once and kept in the table's metadata. Adding one with a *volatile* default, a stored generated column, or an identity column rewrites the whole table and its indexes, which on a large table is exactly the outage this sequence exists to avoid. Older versions rewrote for any default at all, which is why some teams still add columns as nullable by reflex.

questions.prompt: Design the database schema for an audit log recording every change to customer records in a business product. It takes 200 write events per second sustained, must retain events for 7 years, and is queried two ways: everything that happened to one customer, and everything one user did in a given month. Compliance requires that a recorded event is never modified after it is written. Give the tables, keys and indexes, and explain how the design holds up across the retention period.

looks_for: Asks whether the two query paths are interactive or batch/export, and states how the answer changes the design
Asks what is stored per event — a full before/after snapshot, a field-level diff, or only the names of changed fields — and commits to one rather than leaving it open
States that events are append-only and derives a concrete consequence: no update path, no mutable status column, immutability enforced by permissions or by storage choice rather than by convention
Notices that the user-activity query is bounded to a month and uses that bound in the design instead of treating both queries as unbounded

Computes the total event count over the retention period (200/s times roughly 31.5 million seconds per year times 7, so about 4.4 x 10^10 events) rather than reasoning qualitatively about a large volume
Estimates bytes per event and derives total storage from it (for example 500 B per event giving roughly 22 TB), and uses that figure to rule out a single unpartitioned table
Uses the per-day volume (roughly 17 million events per day) to justify the specific partition granularity chosen, rather than picking a granularity by habit
Observes that 200 writes/s is a modest write rate and states explicitly that the design problem is retention volume rather than write throughput
Commits to time-based partitioning, names the granularity, and justifies it from the computed daily volume
Names the index that serves the per-customer query and the index that serves the per-actor query, and recognises that these are two different access paths over the same rows
Proposes moving partitions past a stated age to cheaper storage or an export format, and names what that costs — query latency, loss of SQL access, or both
States how partitions are created and dropped over time as an automated process, rather than treating partitioning as a one-time schema decision

Commits to snapshots or to diffs and states what that costs against the alternative: snapshots cost storage and are trivially readable, diffs cost reconstruction logic and make point-in-time questions expensive
States what the second index costs on an append-only table at this volume, and accepts that cost explicitly rather than adding indexes silently
Names what a partitioned relational table costs against an append-only log or a columnar store for this workload, and commits to one
Takes a position on whether the per-actor query belongs on the same table or needs a separate access path, and states the cost of the position taken
Presents the schema concretely, with named tables, named key columns and named indexes, rather than describing it in prose
States retention and immutability as firm design commitments rather than as open questions for later
Flags which parts of the design would change if the under-specified points were answered differently

questions.model_answer:
A strong answer starts by doing the arithmetic, because the arithmetic is what decides the design. 200 events/s for seven years is roughly 4.4 x 10^10 events; at a few hundred bytes each that is tens of terabytes. Meanwhile 200 writes/s is nothing. Saying this out loud reframes the problem correctly: this is a retention and access-path problem, not a throughput problem.

The core table is a single append-only events table keyed by a generated event id, carrying at minimum the customer id, the acting user id, an event timestamp, an event type, and the payload. It is partitioned by the event timestamp, at a granularity the daily volume justifies — roughly 17 million events per day makes monthly partitions of around half a billion rows, which is large, so a strong answer either goes daily or explains why monthly is acceptable given the storage engine. The per-customer query is served by an index leading with the customer id; the per-actor query is served by a separate index leading with the acting user id, and a strong answer notices that because the query is bounded to a month, that index only needs to be useful within a partition.

On immutability, a strong answer does something structural rather than promising not to run UPDATE: revoking update and delete privileges on the table, or writing to storage that does not support in-place modification. It also explicitly does not add a mutable column such as a status or a soft-delete flag, because that reintroduces the very mutation the requirement forbids.

On growth, a strong answer tiers: recent partitions stay in the operational database, older partitions move to cheaper storage or to an exported columnar format, and the answer says what is lost when they move — usually interactive latency and full SQL. It also treats partition creation and retirement as an automated job rather than a manual task, because over seven years nobody will remember.

The payload decision is the one most candidates skip. Full snapshots make every question answerable and cost storage linearly; field-level diffs cost far less storage but make "what did this record look like on a given date" a replay operation. Either is defensible. What is not defensible is leaving it unstated, because the whole storage estimate depends on it.

A different sound approach is not a worse one. An answer that puts the audit log outside the relational database entirely — an append-only log with a columnar analytical store for both query paths — is at least as good, and arguably better at this volume, provided it addresses immutability, the two access paths, and retention with the same rigour. An answer that keeps everything in one partitioned relational table and justifies it from the modest write rate is also sound. Grade the reasoning and the explicit costing, not the resemblance to the design above.
curveballs: Compliance now requires that any single event be retrievable by id within 200 ms even in year seven, including from the oldest data. Which part of your storage tiering breaks, and what do you change?
Write volume turns out to be bursty: 200/s on average, but 6,000/s for ten minutes whenever a customer runs a bulk import. What happens to your write path and your partitioning during that window?
Legal requires you to delete every event for one customer, to satisfy an erasure request. Your table is append-only and partitioned by time. What do you do, and what does it cost you?

questions.prompt: A team ports an application from MySQL with InnoDB to PostgreSQL without changing any transaction code and without setting an isolation level explicitly. A report that runs several `SELECT` statements inside one transaction used to see a mutually consistent picture, and now sometimes sees rows from different points in time. What explains this?
options: PostgreSQL has no repeatable-read semantics, so the report must become a single query
PostgreSQL's default permits dirty reads, so the report can now see uncommitted rows
PostgreSQL releases read locks at each statement boundary, whereas InnoDB holds them until commit
PostgreSQL's default snapshots each statement, while InnoDB's default snapshots the transaction
questions.explanation:
The two engines have different default isolation levels, and the difference is exactly visible in this symptom. InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, where consistent non-locking reads all share the snapshot established by the transaction's first read — so several `SELECT`s in one transaction are consistent with each other by default. PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED, where each statement takes a fresh snapshot, so two statements in one transaction can legitimately see different committed states. Same code, different default, different behaviour. The fix is to state the level explicitly, which is the durable lesson: never inherit an isolation level you have not chosen.

"PostgreSQL has no repeatable-read semantics" is wrong in an instructive direction. PostgreSQL implements REPEATABLE READ, and its implementation is *stronger* than the SQL standard demands — it forbids phantom reads, which the standard permits at that level, because the standard specifies which anomalies must not occur and exceeding it is conformant. "PostgreSQL's default permits dirty reads" is the misconception the level's name invites; READ COMMITTED means reads see only committed data, and PostgreSQL does not implement READ UNCOMMITTED as a distinct behaviour at all — asking for it gets you READ COMMITTED. "PostgreSQL releases read locks at each statement boundary" attributes the behaviour to locking; both engines serve these reads from multiple row versions and take no read locks, so the difference is the *scope of the snapshot*, not the lifetime of a lock.

What the fix costs, and why READ COMMITTED is a sensible default despite this: a repeatable-read transaction holds its snapshot for its entire life, which prevents reclamation of row versions that were obsoleted after it started. A long-running repeatable-read report is a well-known source of table bloat. It also surfaces serialisation failures that READ COMMITTED silently avoids, so the application must be prepared to retry. For short transactional work, statement-scoped snapshots are cheaper and sufficient — the mistake is running a multi-statement report under them by accident.

resource.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Transaction Isolation Levels

questions.prompt: A messaging product shards its `messages` table across 16 nodes and takes 20,000 writes/s. The dominant read is the most recent 50 messages in one conversation. Measurement shows 0.1% of conversations carry 40% of all messages. Which shard key fits best?
options: `hash(message_id)`, for the most even possible distribution of rows across nodes
`hash(conversation_id)`, so all of one conversation lives on a single node
`hash(conversation_id, time_bucket)`, so one conversation spans a few nodes
`conversation_id` range-partitioned, so adjacent conversations share a node
questions.explanation:
Two requirements pull against each other here. The dominant read wants a conversation's recent messages co-located, which argues for keying on the conversation. The measured skew — one conversation in a thousand carrying four hundred times its share of traffic — makes conversation-only keying produce hot nodes that no amount of rebalancing fixes. Adding a coarse time component resolves the tension: the newest bucket for a conversation serves the recent-50 read from one place, while a high-volume conversation's history spreads across buckets and therefore across nodes.

`hash(conversation_id)` encodes the most common sharding misconception: that hashing the natural entity fixes skew. Hashing distributes *keys* evenly, not *volume*. A single very active conversation hashes to exactly one node and stays there, so the hot key survives the hash untouched. `hash(message_id)` encodes the belief that maximum evenness is the goal; it achieves perfect balance and destroys the only read that matters, turning every recent-50 query into a scatter-gather across all 16 nodes with a merge on top. Range-partitioning on `conversation_id` keeps the hot-key problem and adds a new one — contiguous ranges of identifiers are often correlated with creation time, so newly created conversations cluster onto whichever node holds the high end of the range, and you inherit ongoing range-splitting work.

What the correct answer costs, plainly: the recent-50 read is no longer a single-node lookup in the general case. If the newest bucket holds fewer than 50 messages you must consult the previous one, so the read path needs bucket-boundary logic and may fan out to two or three nodes. You also need a bucket width, and choosing it wrongly either reintroduces hotspots (too wide) or makes every read fan out (too narrow). Writes must compute the bucket consistently, which becomes a compatibility surface.

The assumption that makes this the right answer is that the skew is persistent rather than transient. If the hot conversations were few, stable and identifiable, `hash(conversation_id)` plus a cache in front of those conversations is simpler, keeps every read single-node, and is a perfectly defensible design. The composite key earns its complexity when the hot set is large, shifting, or unpredictable.
questions.source_note: Adapted from the recurring messaging/hot-conversation archetype found across reported interview questions; not attributed to a specific company.
